config.title: Build chaos test for intermittent upstream failures

intro.title: Build chaos test for intermittent upstream failures
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a chaos test that simulates intermittent failures in an upstream service, helping you understand how to make your Node.js applications more resilient. You will learn to use a simple Node.js script to randomly introduce errors or delays, mimicking real-world unreliable network conditions. The core programming concept involves using conditional logic and random number generation to control failure simulation. You will work with basic JavaScript constructs like Math.random(), setTimeout(), and error handling to create and run this test.
intro.usecase: Chaos testing for intermittent upstream failures is essential in distributed systems like e-commerce platforms, payment gateways, and API-driven services. Developers implement this pattern to simulate scenarios where third-party APIs, microservices, or databases become temporarily unavailable, ensuring their applications degrade gracefully. For example, an order processing dashboard might use chaos tests to verify it displays helpful error messages and retry options when the payment service flakes out, rather than crashing entirely. This proactive testing helps build resilient systems that maintain core functionality even during partial outages, directly improving user experience and business continuity.

objectives: Implement a basic Node.js server that simulates intermittent upstream service failures
Configure a chaos testing module to inject random failures into your application
Integrate failure probability controls to manipulate the frequency of simulated outages
Construct a monitoring endpoint to observe the application's behavior during chaos testing
Apply error handling patterns to gracefully manage upstream service disruptions
Initialize a test suite to validate your chaos testing implementation
Render a simple dashboard to visualize failure rates and system responses

steps.instruction: Create a configuration object named 'chaosConfig' with properties for failureRate, timeoutProbability, and errorProbability. Assign numeric values between 0 and 1 to each property.
steps.hint: Define an object with three properties. For example: { failureRate: 0.3, timeoutProbability: 0.2, errorProbability: 0.1 }

steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Define the chaos middleware function
steps.instruction: Define a function called chaosMiddleware that takes a config parameter and returns a middleware function.
steps.hint: The middleware function should have the signature (req, res, next) => { ... } and will contain the chaos injection logic.
steps.expectedOutcome: A chaosMiddleware function is defined that returns a middleware function.

steps.title: Implement random failure injection logic
steps.instruction: Inside your chaosMiddleware function, add logic that uses Math.random() to randomly fail requests based on the configuration's failureRate property.
steps.hint: Generate a random number between 0 and 1 with Math.random(), then compare it to the failureRate value to decide whether to fail the request.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your middleware will now have the core logic to simulate random upstream failures based on the configured failure probability.
successCriteria: The chaosMiddleware function contains logic that uses Math.random() and compares it to a failureRate value to conditionally fail requests.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using Math.random() and comparing it to the failureRate value from your configuration object.
steps.feedbackWrong: The random failure logic isn't implemented correctly. Remember to use Math.random() and compare it to the failureRate to decide when to fail requests.

steps.title: Implement error response simulation
steps.instruction: Inside the chaosMiddleware function, add logic to return random HTTP error responses (500, 502, 503) based on the errorProbability from your configuration.
steps.hint: Generate a random number and compare it to config.errorProbability. If it's less, send a random error status code with a descriptive message.
steps.expectedOutcome: The middleware will now simulate HTTP error responses from upstream services when triggered by the errorProbability.
successCriteria: The chaosMiddleware function includes logic that returns random error status codes (500, 502, 503) based on errorProbability.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using config.errorProbability and returning one of the specified error codes (500, 502, 503).
steps.feedbackWrong: The error simulation logic isn't quite right. Check that you're comparing against config.errorProbability and sending one of the three error status codes.

steps.title: Apply chaos middleware to Express routes
steps.instruction: Use app.use() to apply the chaosMiddleware function to all routes in your Express app, passing your configuration object as an argument.
steps.hint: The app.use() method mounts middleware functions. Pass chaosMiddleware with your configuration object as an argument.

// Similar: applying middleware with configuration
app.use(loggerMiddleware({ level: 'debug' }));
steps.expectedOutcome: The chaosMiddleware will be applied to all incoming requests, enabling chaos testing across your entire Express application.
successCriteria: app.use() is called with chaosMiddleware and the configuration object as arguments.
